concepts.name: Instructions executed in sequence
concepts.summary: Explain that a program is an ordered list of instructions the computer carries out one at a time, top to bottom.

concepts.name: Variables as named storage
concepts.summary: Describe a variable as a named place holding a value that can be read and changed.

concepts.name: Basic data types
concepts.summary: Recognise integers, decimals, text strings and booleans and say what kind of value each holds.

concepts.name: Assignment versus equality
concepts.summary: Distinguish storing a value in a variable from testing whether two values are equal.

concepts.name: Input and output
concepts.summary: Recall how a program receives data from a user and displays results.

concepts.name: Expressions and operators
concepts.summary: Understand how arithmetic and comparison operators combine values into a new value.

misconceptions.text: A variable remembers the formula used to compute it and updates automatically when other variables change.
The = sign in code means the two sides are equal, as in mathematics.
The text "5" and the number 5 are the same thing and behave identically.

concepts.name: Boolean logic and comparisons
concepts.summary: Combine comparisons with and, or and not to write correct conditions.

concepts.name: Conditional branching
concepts.summary: Use if, else if and else to run different code depending on a condition.

concepts.name: Loops for repetition
concepts.summary: Write for and while loops to repeat actions a set number of times or until a condition changes.

concepts.name: Functions and parameters
concepts.summary: Define a function with parameters, call it with arguments and use its return value.

concepts.name: Lists and indexing
concepts.summary: Store several values in a list and access or loop over them by position.

concepts.name: Reading error messages
concepts.summary: Interpret an error message to find the kind of error and the line where it occurred.

concepts.name: Tracing code with print statements
concepts.summary: Insert output statements to observe variable values and find where a program departs from expectations.

misconceptions.text: A loop condition is checked continuously, so a while loop stops the instant the condition becomes false mid-body.
Lists start counting at 1, so the first item is at index 1.
A function that prints a value and a function that returns a value are the same.

concepts.name: Problem decomposition
concepts.summary: Break a problem into smaller subproblems and map each to a function or code block.

concepts.name: Variable scope and lifetime
concepts.summary: Predict where a variable is visible and how long its value persists, including local versus global.

concepts.name: Nested control flow
concepts.summary: Analyse and write combinations of loops and conditions, tracking state across iterations.

concepts.name: Off-by-one and boundary errors
concepts.summary: Identify boundary conditions in loops and indexing and test them deliberately.

concepts.name: Systematic debugging
concepts.summary: Reproduce a bug, form hypotheses, isolate the cause with a debugger or tests, and verify the fix.

concepts.name: Dictionaries and key lookup
concepts.summary: Choose and use key-value structures to associate and retrieve data.

concepts.name: Pass by value versus reference
concepts.summary: Analyse how assigning or passing mutable and immutable values affects whether changes are shared.

concepts.name: Writing simple tests
concepts.summary: Write small checks with expected outputs to confirm a function behaves correctly.

misconceptions.text: Using global variables everywhere is simpler and has no downside.
Copying a list with assignment creates an independent copy.
If a program works on a few typical inputs, it is correct.

concepts.name: Recursion and base cases
concepts.summary: Analyse and write functions that call themselves, identifying base and recursive cases and the call stack.

concepts.name: Error handling strategies
concepts.summary: Judge when to validate input, raise, catch or propagate errors to keep programs robust.

concepts.name: Abstraction and modular design
concepts.summary: Evaluate how code is split into cohesive, loosely coupled functions and modules.

concepts.name: Choosing data structures
concepts.summary: Select among lists, sets, dictionaries and similar structures based on the operations a task needs.

concepts.name: Algorithmic efficiency comparison
concepts.summary: Evaluate alternative approaches by how running time and memory grow with input size.

concepts.name: Refactoring for readability
concepts.summary: Restructure working code and improve naming to reduce duplication without changing behaviour.

concepts.name: Designing test cases
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a test set covers normal, boundary and failure cases.

misconceptions.text: Recursion is always more elegant and efficient than iteration.
Catching and silently ignoring errors makes a program more reliable.
Shorter code is always better code.

concepts.name: Designing for change
concepts.summary: Design program structure so likely future requirements can be added with minimal rework.

concepts.name: Invariants and correctness reasoning
concepts.summary: Use invariants, preconditions and postconditions to argue that code is correct.

concepts.name: Designing debugging strategies
concepts.summary: Create strategies such as bisecting history or inputs and instrumentation to isolate faults in unfamiliar code.

concepts.name: Side effects and state management
concepts.summary: Evaluate how shared mutable state and side effects affect predictability and testing.

concepts.name: Paradigm trade-off evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate procedural, object-oriented and functional styles against a problem's needs.

concepts.name: Teaching and critiquing code
concepts.summary: Review others' code and give reasoned, actionable feedback on correctness, clarity and design.

concepts.name: Creating reusable abstractions
concepts.summary: Create functions or modules with clear interfaces that solve a class of problems rather than one case.

misconceptions.text: One programming paradigm is objectively best for all problems.
Designing for every possible future need up front is good practice.
Passing tests proves a program is correct.
